claims.text: The initial HEA is a single-phase solid solution.
The initial HEA has a homogeneous, compositionally uniform microstructure.
The initial HEA has high ductility.
The baseline HEA has high toughness under standard loading conditions.
High-strain-rate loading near the ductile-to-brittle transition induces localized elemental segregation in the HEA.
Stress-induced segregation or diffusion occurs preferentially along grain boundaries and at dislocation intersections.
Stress-induced elemental segregation nucleates brittle secondary phases or enriched intergranular precipitates.
High mechanical stresses generate localized stress concentrations.
Localized stress concentrations enhance elemental diffusion.
Nanoscale brittle phases form at critical microstructural sites during loading.
Brittle secondary phases or intergranular precipitates act as crack-initiation sites.
Brittle secondary phases provide paths for rapid crack propagation.
Formation of brittle secondary phases reduces fracture toughness.
Loaded specimens will fail in a brittle manner earlier than the initial baseline under comparable loading.
The proposed embrittlement mechanism activates at high strain rates and temperatures near the HEA's ductile-to-brittle transition.
Low or variable temperatures and cyclic fatigue can provide conditions sufficient to activate segregation and secondary-phase formation.
Conventional deformation mechanisms cease to sustain toughness beyond the proposed loading and temperature boundary.
Diffraction and TEM can be used during mechanical testing to investigate phase and microstructural evolution.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis requires segregation to cause brittle secondary-phase or precipitate nucleation, whereas the predicted outcome treats segregation and phase formation as alternatives ('and/or'), allowing segregation alone to count as the expected mediator.

The predicted mechanical outcome calls for comparison under similar loading conditions, but the stated control is an as-cast, untested baseline rather than a matched specimen tested at a lower strain rate or outside the transition-temperature range. This leaves loading exposure confounded with the proposed high-rate mechanism.
